title: Market Day in Villa de Leyva
paragraphs: Ana lives in Villa de Leyva, a small town in Boyacá, Colombia. Every Saturday, she goes to the market with her grandfather, Don Luis. The market is in a big square near the church. It opens at seven o'clock in the morning.

The market is very busy. There are many stalls with fruit, vegetables, cheese and bread. Ana loves the colors. There are red tomatoes, yellow bananas and green avocados. People talk and laugh, and a man plays the guitar.

Don Luis buys potatoes, onions and a big piece of white cheese. Ana buys six oranges and a bag of strawberries. She pays with a ten thousand peso note. The woman at the stall gives her the change and a free mango!
At ten o'clock, Ana and her grandfather sit on a bench and eat arepas with cheese. Ana is happy. Saturday is her favorite day of the week.

title: The Capybara: A Big, Friendly Rodent
paragraphs: The capybara is the biggest rodent in the world. A rodent is an animal like a mouse or a rat. But a capybara is not small! It can weigh 50 kilos, about the same as a person. In Colombia, people call it 'chigüiro'.
Capybaras live in South America, in hot places near rivers and lakes. You can see many capybaras in the Llanos, the big flat plains of Colombia and Venezuela.

Capybaras love water. They are very good swimmers. Their eyes, ears and nose are on the top of their head, so they can see and breathe in the water. They can stay under the water for about five minutes.
Capybaras eat grass and water plants. They live in groups of ten or twenty animals. They are calm and quiet, and other animals, like birds, often sit on their backs!

title: A Day with a Bus Driver
paragraphs: Rosa Mosquera is a bus driver in Cali. She is 38 years old. We ask her about her job.
What time do you start work? I start very early. I get up at four o'clock, and my first bus leaves at five thirty.
Do you like your job? Yes, I love it! I drive the same route every day, and I know many passengers. Some children say 'Good morning, Rosa!' every day. That makes me happy.
Is your job difficult? Sometimes. The traffic in the afternoon is terrible, and I sit for many hours. But I have a break at eleven, and I eat lunch with the other drivers.
What do you do after work? I finish at two o'clock. Then I go home and help my son with his homework. In the evening, I go dancing salsa with my husband. Cali is the city of salsa!

title: Sundays in Bogotá
paragraphs: Hi everyone! My name is Sofía and this is my blog about Bogotá. Today I want to tell you about Sundays in my city.

On Sunday mornings, many big streets in Bogotá close to cars. They are only for bikes, skates and people on foot. This is the Ciclovía. It starts at seven in the morning and finishes at two in the afternoon.

I ride my bike with my dad. We start near our house and go to a big park. There are thousands of people: children, grandparents, dogs and even cats in baskets! Some people do exercise classes in the street.

We stop for a fresh orange juice and a snack. My favorite snack is a mango with salt and lemon. Then we ride home. I am tired but happy. Do you have something like the Ciclovía in your city? Write in the comments!

title: Five Easy Breakfasts
paragraphs: Breakfast is an important meal. It gives you energy for school or work. But many people say, 'I don't have time!' Here are five easy breakfasts. You can make each one in ten minutes or less.
1. Arepa with egg. Cook an egg in a pan and put it on a warm arepa. It is simple and delicious. 2. Fruit and yogurt. Cut a banana and some papaya. Put the fruit in a bowl with yogurt.
3. Oatmeal. Cook oats with milk for five minutes. Add cinnamon and a little honey. 4. Toast with avocado. Put avocado on brown bread with salt and lemon.
5. A smoothie. Put milk, a banana and some strawberries in a blender. Drink it in a glass or take it to school in a bottle.
Tip: Drink a glass of water in the morning too. And remember: sweet cakes and soda are not a good breakfast every day!

title: Mariana Pajón: Queen of BMX
paragraphs: Mariana Pajón was born in Medellín, Colombia, in 1991. When she was a little girl, she watched her father and her older brother at BMX races, and she wanted to race too. She started riding a BMX bike when she was only four years old, and she was often the only girl in the race.

BMX is a fast and dangerous sport. Riders race on a short track with jumps and tight turns. Mariana fell many times and broke some bones, but she never stopped. She trained harder than the other riders, and she won many races in Colombia and in other countries.

In 2012, she went to the Olympic Games in London and won the gold medal in women's BMX. Many people in Colombia watched the race on TV and celebrated in the streets. Four years later, in Rio de Janeiro, she won gold again. Then, at the Olympic Games in Tokyo, she won a silver medal.
Today, people call her 'the Queen of BMX'. Many young Colombians, especially girls, started riding BMX because of her. Her story shows that falling is part of learning.

title: The Phone on the Bus
paragraphs: Last Tuesday, Julián was going home from school on the bus. It was raining and the bus was full. He was listening to music and looking out of the window. When the bus stopped near the university, a young woman got off quickly. Julián looked down and saw a phone on the seat next to him.

He picked it up. It was an expensive phone, much newer than his old one. For a moment, he thought, 'Nobody saw it. I can keep it.' But then he remembered last year, when he lost his own wallet. He felt terrible for days.

Suddenly the phone started ringing. On the screen it said 'Mom'. Julián answered. 'Hello? Sorry, I found this phone on the bus.' The woman was very relieved. She explained that her daughter, Laura, was a student at the university. They decided to meet the next day at a café near Julián's school.

The next afternoon, Laura arrived at the café with her mother. She was so happy to see her phone. 'All my photos are on it,' she said. She wanted to give Julián some money, but he said no. Instead, Laura bought him a hot chocolate and a big piece of cake. 'This is better than money,' Julián laughed.

title: The Flower Festival of Medellín
paragraphs: Every August, the city of Medellín becomes a garden. For about ten days, there are concerts, dances, food stalls and parades all over the city. This is the Feria de las Flores, or Flower Festival, and it started in 1957.

The most famous part of the festival is the Silleteros Parade. Silleteros are farmers from Santa Elena, a rural area in the mountains near the city. They make huge flower designs on wooden frames called silletas, and they carry them on their backs. Some silletas are very heavy. They can weigh as much as an adult person!

Long ago, before there were good roads, people in Santa Elena used silletas to carry things down the mountain. Later, farmers used them to bring flowers to sell in the city. Today, silleteros spend weeks preparing their designs. Some show birds, national symbols or messages of peace. Grandparents teach the work to their children and grandchildren.

There are other events too, like a parade of old and classic cars. Thousands of tourists visit the city during the festival, so hotels are often full. If you are going to visit, it is a good idea to book early!

title: My First Month in Dublin
paragraphs: Hi! It's Lucía again. I arrived in Dublin, Ireland, exactly one month ago. I'm studying English at a language school here for six months. My friends in Arequipa keep asking me, 'How is it?' So here is my answer!

The first week was hard. When I arrived, it was raining and very cold, colder than any winter in Arequipa! I didn't understand the bus drivers because they speak very fast, and I got lost twice. I was also a bit lonely at first.

But things are better now. I live with a host family, the Byrnes. They have two kids and a very lazy cat. Mrs Byrne makes a big dinner every evening, and we talk about our day. My English is improving fast because I have to speak it all the time.

My classmates come from Brazil, Japan, Turkey and Spain. Last weekend we went to the coast together. We walked on the cliffs, and the sea was beautiful but very windy. Then we ate fish and chips on the beach.

Next month, I'm going to look for a part-time job in a café. I'm a bit nervous, but I'm going to try! I miss my mum's cooking, though. Irish potatoes are good, but nothing is better than her rocoto relleno.

title: Should Teenagers Get Pocket Money?
paragraphs: Many parents give their children a small amount of money every week or month. In English, this is called 'pocket money'. Some people think it is a great idea, but others don't agree. I'm Andrés, I'm sixteen, and this is my opinion.

I think pocket money is important because it teaches you how to manage money. When I was thirteen, my parents started giving me 20,000 pesos a week. At first, I spent everything on snacks and video games in two days. Then I had nothing for the rest of the week! It was a hard lesson, but a useful one.

Now I'm more careful. I write down what I spend in a notebook, and I save a little every week. Last year, I saved enough money to buy a second-hand guitar. That felt much better than asking my parents for it.

Of course, not all families can give pocket money, and that's OK. Some teenagers earn money by helping neighbors, for example by walking dogs or washing cars. Other people say that children should help at home for free, not for money. I agree with that. I don't get paid for washing the dishes!
In my opinion, a small amount of pocket money is a good way to learn. Mistakes with small amounts are cheaper than mistakes with big amounts later in life.

title: Volunteers Help Baby Turtles Reach the Sea
paragraphs: Last weekend, more than 300 baby sea turtles walked across the sand and into the Caribbean Sea at Playa Escondida. It was a happy moment for a group of volunteers who protected the turtle eggs for almost two months.

Earlier this year, several female turtles came to the beach at night and laid their eggs in the sand. Local fishermen saw them and called a small environmental group. The volunteers, most of them students from the town's high school, put a fence around the nests. They also took turns watching the beach every night.

Sea turtles have many problems. Plastic is very dangerous for them, because they think plastic bags are jellyfish and eat them. Lights are another problem. Baby turtles move toward the brightest light. Usually this is the moon over the sea, but sometimes it is a street lamp, so they walk the wrong way.

'We were very tired after many nights on the beach, but it was worth it,' said Mateo Ruiz, 17, one of the volunteers. The group is now going to visit schools to teach children about turtles. They also want restaurants near the beach to turn off their lights at night.

title: Why Do We Dream?
paragraphs: Every night, most of us spend about two hours dreaming, even if we don't remember it in the morning. Over a lifetime, that adds up to around six years. For thousands of years, people have tried to explain dreams. Some ancient cultures believed they were messages from the gods, while others thought they could predict the future. Today, scientists have better tools to study them, but they still haven't found a complete answer.

What we do know is that most vivid dreams happen during a stage of sleep called REM, which stands for 'rapid eye movement'. During REM sleep, our eyes move quickly under the eyelids, and our brain is almost as active as when we are awake. At the same time, most of the muscles in our body are temporarily switched off. Researchers believe this stops us from acting out our dreams, for example running or kicking while we are still in bed.

There are several theories about why we dream. One popular idea is that dreams help the brain to organise memories. During the day, we receive huge amounts of information, and sleep may be the time when the brain decides what to keep and what to forget. Another theory suggests that dreams allow us to practise dealing with threats in a safe environment, which could explain why so many dreams involve being chased or falling.

Dreams may also be connected to our emotions. Studies have shown that people who are going through a stressful period often have more negative dreams. If you have ever dreamt about an exam you hadn't studied for, you are certainly not alone.

So, should you pay attention to your dreams? Scientists say they are not secret codes, but they can tell us something about what is on our mind. If you want to remember them better, try keeping a notebook next to your bed and writing them down as soon as you wake up.

title: Katherine Johnson: Counting to the Moon
paragraphs: Long before computers were small enough to fit in our pockets, the word 'computer' described a job, not a machine. In the 1950s, 'computers' were people, very often women, who did complex mathematical calculations by hand. One of the most brilliant of them was Katherine Johnson, whose work helped send the first Americans into space.

Johnson was born in 1918 in West Virginia, in the United States. From an early age, she was fascinated by numbers and counted everything around her. She was so talented that she finished high school at 14 and graduated from university at 18. However, opportunities for a Black woman in science were extremely limited at that time, so she worked as a teacher for several years.

In 1953, she was hired by the organisation that later became NASA. At first, Black women mathematicians were made to work in a separate office, because the laws of the time kept Black and white people apart. Johnson refused to let this stop her. She asked questions, went to meetings where women were not usually invited, and soon earned the respect of the engineers.

Her calculations were essential for the flight of Alan Shepard, the first American in space, in 1961. A year later, before John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth, the astronaut insisted that she personally check the numbers produced by the new electronic computers. She also worked on calculations for the Apollo 11 mission, which took humans to the Moon in 1969.

For many years, her contribution was almost unknown to the public. That changed in 2015, when she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and in 2016, when the film Hidden Figures told her story. Johnson died in 2020 at the age of 101, but she remains an inspiration for young people who dream of careers in science.

title: Homework: Help or Headache?
paragraphs: Few topics cause as many arguments in schools as homework. Students complain that they spend their evenings doing worksheets instead of resting, while many parents and teachers insist that homework is essential for success. I have been a secondary school teacher in Cali for eight years, and I have changed my mind about this question more than once.

There are good arguments in favour of homework. Practising at home helps students remember what they have learned in class, especially in subjects like maths and languages, where repetition really matters. Homework can also teach young people to organise their time and work independently, skills they will need at university and at work.

However, I have seen the other side too. Many of my students take long bus journeys, help their families after school or have part-time jobs. When they are given two or three hours of homework every night, they arrive at class exhausted. Some simply copy answers from a classmate or an app, which means the homework teaches them nothing.

So what is the answer? I don't think homework should be banned, but I believe it should be shorter and more meaningful. If a task takes twenty minutes and makes students think, for example reading a short article, interviewing a grandparent or solving one interesting problem, it is far more valuable than fifty repetitive exercises. Since I started giving less homework, my students have actually completed more of it, and the quality has improved.
Rest, family time and sport are also part of a good education. Homework should support learning, not replace a healthy life.

title: Students Turn Plastic Bottles into Water Filters
paragraphs: A group of teenagers from La Esperanza, a small rural town in northern Colombia, have won a national science prize for a low-cost water filter that is made almost entirely from recycled materials. The filter, which was designed by five students aged 15 to 17, could help families who do not have regular access to clean drinking water.

The project began last year, after heavy rains damaged the town's water system. 'For weeks, people had to boil every drop of water they drank, and gas is expensive,' explained Valeria Mena, 16, one of the team members. 'Some families couldn't afford it, and some children got sick. We wanted to find a solution that anyone could build at home.'

The filter is built from a large plastic bottle that has been cut in half. Inside, the water passes through several layers: small stones, sand, charcoal and a piece of clean cotton cloth. Each layer removes a different kind of dirt. In the final step, the filtered water is left in a clear bottle in direct sunlight for at least six hours, a method that is known to kill many harmful bacteria.

With help from their chemistry teacher, the students tested water samples at a university laboratory in the nearest city. The results showed that the system removed most of the dirt and a large percentage of the bacteria. However, the team is careful to point out that their filter is not perfect. 'If the water has chemicals in it, our filter won't remove them,' Valeria said.

The prize includes 20 million pesos, which the students plan to use to build 200 filters for local families. They have also recorded a short video with step-by-step instructions so that people in other communities can make their own.

title: Inside the Job of a Game Designer
paragraphs: Camila Fuentes, 29, grew up in Santiago, Chile, and now works as a game designer for an independent studio in Montreal, Canada. Her latest game, a puzzle adventure set in the Andes, has been downloaded more than half a million times. We asked her what the job is really like.

Many teenagers dream of making video games. How did you get started? Honestly, by accident. I studied graphic design at university because I loved drawing. In my third year, a friend who was studying computer science asked me to help with the art for a small game. We worked on it every weekend for six months. It was never sold, but I discovered that I loved creating worlds that people could walk through.

What does a game designer actually do? People think we play games all day, which isn't true! A designer decides how the game works: the rules, the levels, what the player can do and why it's fun. I write a lot of documents, I draw maps on paper and I spend hours in meetings with programmers and artists. Then we test everything again and again. If players get bored or confused, we have to change it.

What is the hardest part of the job? Deadlines. Before a game is released, the team often works very long hours. I've also learned that most of your ideas won't work. You have to be ready to throw away something you've spent weeks on.

What advice would you give to young people who want to do this job? Don't wait for permission. There are free tools online, so start making small games now, even if they are simple. Finish them and show them to people. And study things outside games too, like history, music or psychology. The best ideas often come from somewhere unexpected.

title: How to Prepare for Your First Job Interview
paragraphs: Your first job interview can feel frightening, whether it is for a weekend job in a shop or an internship at a big company. The good news is that interviews are a skill, and like any skill, they can be learned. If you follow these steps, you will feel much more confident when the day arrives.

1. Research the company. Find out what the company does, who its customers are and what it believes in. Interviewers are often impressed when candidates can explain why they want to work for that particular company, not just any company.

2. Prepare your stories. Most interviewers will ask questions like 'Tell me about a time you solved a problem.' Even if you have never had a job, you can use examples from school projects, sports teams or volunteering. Describe the situation, what you did and what the result was.

3. Practise out loud. Ask a friend or family member to play the role of the interviewer. It may feel strange, but saying your answers out loud is very different from thinking them. You could also record yourself on your phone to check whether you speak too fast.

4. Plan the practical details. Check the address and how long it takes to get there, and aim to arrive ten minutes early. Choose clean, appropriate clothes the night before. If the interview is online, test your camera, microphone and internet connection in advance.

5. Ask your own questions. At the end, you will probably be asked if you have any questions. Always have one or two ready, such as 'What does a typical day look like in this job?' This shows that you are genuinely interested.
Finally, remember that an interview is a conversation, not an exam. Even if you don't get the job, every interview is good practice for the next one.

title: The Real Cost of Fast Fashion
paragraphs: A T-shirt for the price of a sandwich, a new pair of jeans every month: for many shoppers, fashion has never been cheaper or easier to buy. This is the world of 'fast fashion', in which big brands copy catwalk styles and produce them quickly and cheaply, sometimes releasing new collections every week. But while the prices on the labels are low, the real cost is often paid by someone else.

First, there is the environment. Clothing production uses huge amounts of water and energy. It has been estimated that making a single cotton T-shirt can require around 2,700 litres of water. Many cheap clothes are made from polyester, a type of plastic, which releases tiny fibres into rivers and oceans every time it is washed.

Then there is the problem of waste. Because clothes are so cheap, people tend to wear them only a few times before throwing them away. Enormous piles of unwanted clothing have been dumped in places such as the Atacama Desert in northern Chile.

Finally, there are the workers. A lot of fast fashion is made in factories in countries such as Bangladesh, where wages are low and conditions can be dangerous. In 2013, more than 1,100 people died when the Rana Plaza building, which contained several clothing factories, collapsed near the capital, Dhaka.

So what can ordinary shoppers do? Some experts suggest asking a simple question before buying anything: 'Will I wear this at least thirty times?' Buying second-hand clothes, swapping with friends and learning to repair small holes are other options. In many Latin American cities, second-hand markets and online groups have become popular among young people, who see them as both cheaper and cooler. If we all bought fewer, better clothes and kept them for longer, the difference could be enormous.

title: Film Review: The Last Garden
paragraphs: The Last Garden, directed by Inés Arango. My rating: four stars out of five.

It is the year 2090, and most of the planet has turned into desert. In a small research station in the Colombian Andes, a scientist called Elena guards the last seed bank on Earth: thousands of seeds that could, in theory, bring back the world's lost forests. When a group of strangers arrives asking for shelter, Elena has to decide who she can trust.

This is the second feature film by Arango, whose first film, a quiet documentary about coffee farmers, was praised at several international festivals. The Last Garden is far more ambitious, but she hasn't lost her eye for small human details. Some of the most powerful scenes have no action at all: Elena talking to her plants, or teaching a frightened child how to plant a bean.

The film was shot almost entirely in the páramo near Bogotá, and the photography is stunning. The strange, silvery frailejón plants, which only grow in a few places in the world, make the landscape look like another planet. The soundtrack, which mixes electronic music with traditional Andean flutes, is equally memorable.

However, the film isn't perfect. The second half moves too slowly, and some of the strangers are not developed enough, so it's hard to care about what happens to them. The ending, which I won't spoil here, may also divide audiences: some will find it hopeful, while others will find it too sudden.
Overall, The Last Garden is a beautiful and thoughtful film. If you prefer fast action, you might be disappointed, but if you enjoy films that make you think, it's definitely worth watching.

title: The Night the Lights Went Out
paragraphs: Tomás had lived in his apartment building in Buenos Aires for three years, but he could only name two of his neighbours. Like most people in the building, he left early for work, came back late and spent his evenings looking at a screen. The neighbours nodded at each other in the lift, and that was all.

Then, one hot evening in January, the power went out across the whole neighbourhood. At first, Tomás waited for the lights to come back on. After an hour, his phone battery was almost dead, the apartment was unbearably hot, and he was beginning to feel anxious. Through the open window, he could hear voices in the courtyard below.

He went downstairs with a candle. To his surprise, about twenty people were already there. Mrs Ferreyra from the fourth floor, who he had always thought was rather unfriendly, had brought out a camping stove and was making mate for everyone. A teenager he had never noticed was playing the guitar, and two small children were running around with torches, delighted by the adventure.

Someone suggested that everyone should bring the food from their fridges before it went bad. Soon there was a long table covered with cheese, empanadas, fruit and half-melted ice cream. People who had lived next to each other for years introduced themselves for the first time. Tomás discovered that the quiet man from the sixth floor was a retired history teacher, and that Mrs Ferreyra laughed louder than anyone he knew.

The electricity came back just after midnight. Everyone cheered, but nobody went upstairs immediately. Before they said goodnight, someone created a group chat for the building. Since then, the neighbours have organised a dinner in the courtyard every month. Tomás sometimes jokes that the blackout was the best thing that has ever happened to the building.

title: A Complaint About an Online Order
paragraphs: Subject: Order 48213, damaged item and request for a refund. Dear Customer Service Team,

I am writing to complain about a laptop that I ordered from your website on 2 September. I was promised delivery within five working days, but the package did not arrive until 19 September, almost two weeks later than expected. During that time, I contacted your customer service line three times, and on each occasion I was told that the order had been sent, but nobody could tell me where it was.

When the package was finally delivered, the box had clearly been damaged. I opened it immediately and found that the laptop screen was cracked in the top corner. I have attached photographs of both the box and the screen, as well as a copy of my receipt.

I need this laptop for my university course, which started on 15 September, so the delay has caused me serious problems. I have had to borrow a computer from a friend in order to complete my first assignments.

According to the returns policy on your website, customers who receive damaged products are entitled to a full refund or a replacement. I would therefore like to request a full refund of 2,150,000 pesos, paid to the credit card that I used for the purchase. I would also be grateful if you could arrange for the damaged laptop to be collected from my address, as I do not have a car.
If I have not received a reply within ten working days, I will contact the consumer protection authority. I hope this will not be necessary, and I look forward to hearing from you soon.
Yours faithfully, Daniela Ospina
